title: Finley v. United States (1989)
summary: The Court required statutory authorization before adding private defendants to the federal tort claim against the United States.
notes:
Do not apply Finley as though § 1367 had never been enacted. Its principal course role is to explain the need for and design of the later supplemental-jurisdiction statute.

Facts and posture: Finley's husband and children died when their plane struck power lines approaching a San Diego airfield; she sued the United States under the FTCA for FAA negligence, then moved to add state-law claims against the City of San Diego and the utility; the district court allowed it under Gibbs, the Ninth Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court (Scalia, J.) affirmed.

The decision was 5–4: Justice Blackmun dissented, and Justice Stevens dissented joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall.

sections.Parties: Finley sued the United States concerning an aviation accident and sought related recovery from additional local or private defendants.
sections.Material Facts: The accident involved an aircraft and power lines near an airfield. The Federal Tort Claims Act supplied the claim against the United States. The plaintiff sought to combine that claim with related claims against other entities involved in the same event. The strong factual relationship did not resolve whether the federal jurisdictional statute permitted bringing those parties into the action.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected pendent-party jurisdiction under the statute as it then stood. Congress subsequently enacted § 1367, which the course studies as the statutory response.
sections.Issue: Was a common constitutional case enough to support the additional defendants without an affirmative statutory grant?
sections.Holding: No, under the pre-§ 1367 statutory framework applied in Finley.
sections.Reasoning: Federal adjudicatory authority requires both constitutional permission and statutory authorization. The Court read the Federal Tort Claims Act’s jurisdictional grant as directed to claims against the United States and declined to infer jurisdiction over additional parties merely from their connection to the same occurrence. The resulting fragmentation was a policy consequence Congress could address.

learning.why: The Court required statutory authorization before adding private defendants to the federal tort claim against the United States.

topics.cp-pendent-parties: Constitutional factual relatedness did not itself supply congressional authorization for new-party claims.
topics.cp-supplemental-history: Congress’s later § 1367 responded to the restrictive pendent-party approach.
topics.cp-usc-1367: Section 1367 was enacted in 1990 specifically to overrule Finley, and § 1367(a) authorizes joinder of additional parties.

mnemonic.rationale: A plane that hit power lines
